prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, and models of dynamic industries, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the measurement of market power and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single achievement, B001, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons but did not change the slate. The chair asks what separates a methods-and-tools contribution from a substantive discovery. I would use four tests, the same for every field. First, did the contribution make something measurable that was not measurable before? Second, did it change how decisions are made outside academia? Third, did it spread beyond its home field? Fourth, did it survive sustained critique? Random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995) and the dynamic-industry framework pass all four on the evidence cited in round 1. They give substitution patterns, markups and welfare counterfactuals that reduced-form work could not. They are used in merger review, antitrust and regulation. They have spread to trade, health, environmental and public economics. The numerical and identification problems have been studied intensively for three decades. I come from corporate finance, where contract theory became a discipline once it was tested against real contracts, so I do not treat theory-meets-data tools as craft in a pejorative sense. The citation should name the method and the dynamic-industry framework, say nothing about robustness, and not try to cover production-function estimation or the wider new empirical IO programme. On the second-achievement question I raised in round 1, I now think a single part is best. Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn use all three laureate slots, so a second part would force a two-name B001 that splits the BLP authors. The only way to fit a second part would be to weaken the one achievement the Committee can cite most precisely. I do not ask for an artificial second part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still that this honours a toolkit, and a Committee that wants only substantive findings could reasonably choose B013 or B002. The pooled entry also leaves attribution open. Bresnahan founded the new empirical IO programme, and a programme-level citation would credit him and probably not Levinsohn. Any three-name cut leaves out Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I also concede that I am relying on background knowledge for adoption, regulatory-use and sensitivity claims, and the exchange has not supplied independent evidence for them. Applied BLP estimates can depend on optimiser tolerance, instrument choice and functional form, and I cannot say from the supplied material how often those choices have changed a real merger or welfare conclusion.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan instead of Levinsohn beside Pakes and Berry. He argues that Bresnahan's new empirical IO and early differentiated-product demand and market-power work supplied the question the later tools answered. He accepts that a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I agree this is the real fault line, and I accept that Bresnahan's claim to the programme is large. I still choose Levinsohn, for a reason of citation design and not of merit. The achievement the Committee can describe most exactly is estimating demand with endogenous prices and equilibrium supply, and that is a specific jointly authored result. Leaving out Levinsohn while crediting Berry would split its authors. A programme-level citation is a different prize with a more diffuse boundary, where Reiss, Benkard and Levin would also have to be weighed. The chair asked whether each supporter would accept the other framing's third name. I would accept Bresnahan only if the Committee deliberately chose the programme-level framing, and then the citation would have to be rewritten, not merely have a name swapped. I do not think the evidence in the exchange settles the choice.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She argues it pairs an explanatory framework (Katz-Murphy relative demand and the task approach) with transparent new designs on local labour-market adjustment. She accepts B001 is the strongest alternative and says the Katz versus Dorn choice is a real judgement call.
responses.response: I take her argument seriously, and B013 remains my first alternative. The framework-plus-design combination is real and the policy relevance is large. Two things keep it second for me. The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects is still contested, and I cannot judge from this exchange how settled it is. The three-name cap also forces a choice between Katz and Dorn that Hjalmarsson herself calls a judgement. B001 has no comparable split in its core credit. I agree with her that first-place counts are not evidence of merit. My ranking rests on whether the work has been tested, and a three-decade record of use and critique is a stronger basis than a decade-old strand that is still being revised.

responses.point: Friberg treats the contribution as a measurement discovery that changed what economists can say about substitution, markups and welfare. He would keep the citation on demand estimation and market power and leave the dynamic-oligopoly and production-function work as supporting context.
responses.response: I agree with the measurement framing and with its use of the chair's toolkit question. Where we differ slightly is the dynamic-industry strand. I would keep a short reference to dynamic-industry models in the citation, because Pakes's credit rests partly on that framework and it explains why he anchors the trio. I would not extend it to production-function estimation or entry models. That keeps the unit narrow, as Hassler also urged, and avoids reopening attribution among Reiss, Benkard, Levin and others. If the Committee prefers Friberg's narrower wording, it does not change who is credited, so I would not treat the difference as material.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved his preferred part from B002 to B001. He keeps B002 as a strong alternative and says his own B002 trio, with Gertler, is now less secure given the Kiyotaki-Moore pair and the 2022 overlap.
responses.response: I share his reasoning and revise one thing in light of it. In round 1 I left Gertler's inclusion in B002 open to argument. After the convergent statements from Hassler, Krusell, Boppart and Teorell, I would now support only the Kiyotaki-Moore pair if the Committee turned to B002. Adding Gertler brings in the accelerator strand, which runs through Bernanke and overlaps the 2022 prize. If B002 advances I would ask for a citation that says explicitly what is distinct from the banks-and-crises prize, namely collateral-constraint amplification of shocks. I note that this refinement affects only my second alternative and does not move my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B013 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz. She argues that technology and trade strands are linked through Autor, that debate has refined and not overturned the central patterns, and that a methods toolkit should not automatically outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution.
responses.response: I agree that a toolkit should not automatically outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution, and my case does not depend on that. B001 should win only if it passes the common tests, and I think it does. I accept her point that debate has refined and not overturned B013's patterns. The difference for me is attribution and timing, not whether the work is good. Two linked strands, with the third slot contested between Katz and Dorn, make a three-name citation harder to write cleanly than for BLP. I would be comfortable with B013 as a later prize, and I keep it as my first alternative for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee adopts a method-level or programme-level citation, which would decide between Levinsohn and Bresnahan for the third slot. I do not think the supplied material settles it.
Whether the Committee treats a measurement capability as a sufficient discovery, and how it would weigh B001 against B013 if it applies the toolkit-versus-discovery test strictly.

How often numerical implementation, instrument choice or functional-form assumptions have changed a real merger or welfare conclusion. I can only reason from background knowledge here. Systematic evidence on this would change how much weight I put on applied reliability, and the chair's question about it is a fair one.
Whether the China-shock magnitudes in B013 and the distinct ground left by the 2022 prize for B002 are firm enough to rank those ahead of B001 at a later date.
I have not independently verified any citation, adoption or regulatory-use claim in this exchange.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from my profile and disclosed, not adjudicated. I am a corporate-finance researcher, and my listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) are not credited on B001, B013 or B002. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth, but I see no tie to a credited name on those entries. I am also Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. The profile records long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson. Hassler and Krusell are B001 supporters, and I have tried to answer their positions on the merits. I work close to B012, which I ranked fourth in my opening and do not propose. My presentation speeches as chair do not establish a prize preference.
